questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the most common mistake engineers make with the shared responsibility model?
options: Treating it as a fixed 50/50 split instead of a line that moves depending on the service model
Assuming AWS and Azure use completely incompatible responsibility models
Believing that the customer is always responsible for 100% of security
Thinking the provider is never responsible for anything once a VM is deployed
questions.explain: The model isn't a fixed split — the responsibility line slides up the stack depending on whether the service is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.

questions.q: For an IaaS service like an Azure VM or AWS EC2 instance, which of the following is the customer's responsibility?
options: Securing the physical datacenter
Guest OS patching and network configuration such as NSGs or security groups
Managing the hypervisor
Patching the host hardware firmware
questions.explain: For IaaS, the provider secures the physical infrastructure and hypervisor; the customer owns everything from the guest OS up, including patching and network rules.

questions.q: Moving from IaaS to PaaS (e.g., from an EC2 instance to RDS, or from an Azure VM to Azure SQL Database) does what to the responsibility line?
options: It removes the customer's responsibility entirely
It has no effect — the line stays identical
It makes the customer responsible for patching the database engine directly
It shifts more of the stack (OS patching, engine management) onto the provider, leaving the customer with data, access, and service configuration
questions.explain: PaaS moves the line up: the provider now manages the OS and engine, while the customer is left responsible for data, identity/access configuration, and service-level settings like firewall rules.

questions.q: Why do CIS Benchmarks for Azure and AWS focus almost entirely on customer-side controls rather than provider infrastructure?
options: Because those controls sit on the customer's side of the shared responsibility line, which is the part the customer can actually configure and is accountable for
Because CIS Benchmarks are not aware that cloud providers exist
Because provider infrastructure has no security controls worth checking
Because customer-side controls are easier to write test scripts for, with no relation to responsibility
questions.explain: CIS Benchmarks check things like Entra ID MFA enforcement, storage account public access, and logging configuration because those are the controls on the customer's side of the responsibility line — the provider's infrastructure security is a contractual obligation, not something the customer audits.

questions.q: What should you do before deploying a new Azure or AWS service to correctly understand your responsibility for it?
options: Assume every PaaS service has an identical responsibility boundary
Skip the documentation since the shared responsibility model is the same for every service
Find that specific service's security baseline or shared-responsibility documentation, since boundaries differ even within the same category
Only check responsibility boundaries after an incident occurs
questions.explain: The lesson stresses confirming the boundary for the specific service — e.g., AWS Lambda's boundary (code and IAM execution role vs. AWS-managed runtime) differs meaningfully from EC2's, even though both sit in different categories.
